speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say, in rising to speak on this most important motion before us, that I intend to be exceedingly brief. Members who have spoken before me have fully and adequately conveyed almost all my thoughts and sentiments on matters affecting the veterans of this country. May I say that about the only thing with which I disagree, is the confidence in the Minister of Veterans
October 27, 1970

Affairs (Mr. Dube) expressed by the previous speaker. I am not prepared to give him a vote of confidence until we have action, not excuses, legislation and not a series of promises. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, and it is only after action that the minister will be entitled to a strong expression of confidence. I hope the time is not too distant when I, too, can express confidence in the minister.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Without any fear of contradiction, I can say I feel certain hon. members of the House are unanimous concerning the need for changes in the legislation, changes in the regulations and changes in policy. Because I am so strongly convinced that statement is correct, I shall not take the time to repeat what has already been said concerning the excellence of the work of the Woods commission and the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. I believe it is obvious that the only thing that requires repetition is that in the time available as many of us as possible should express to the minister and the government our belief that there is a matter of urgency involved and a need for action. I most certainly agree with hon. members who have said this is a matter of top priority. It certainly is in the constituency of Vancouver East.
There are thousands of veterans in Vancouver East, and thousands of them are members of veterans organizations such as the Royal Canadian Legion and the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans of Canada. All the time they say: when, oh when, is something going to be done? Is the government delaying because month by month and year by year so many of us are dying that there will be fewer and fewer in respect of whom the government will have to accept a greater financial responsibility? This is what the veterans are saying, everybody knows it. I think it is shameful that it should be necessary for our veterans to engage in this type of thinking. It certainly is necessary, however, when we realize that the studies were first commenced over five years ago and we are still awaiting the legislation from the government.
I said I would not repeat what has already been brought to the attention of the minister and the government, but I should like to add the thought that I hope in his deliberations the minister is prepared not only to bring in legislation dealing with the Hong Kong veterans but also Canadian prisoners of war in other areas. One only has to speak to the veterans, as I do so often being a member of both the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans of Canada and the Royal Canadian Legion, to be aware of the effects of the imprisonment, starvation and hell they went through in the camps in Europe, some of them for long periods. I believe this merits immediate consideration. I hope the government will keep this in mind.
I most certainly hope there will be immediate action to resolve a great many of the veterans problems which are brought to the attention of Members of Parliament. I refer of course in particular to the vicious, pressing situation surrounding those who of necessity receive the
Veterans Allowance Increases War Veterans Allowance. This has been mentioned by many members, particularly by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). However, I wish to add my plea for immediate action in this regard because of the numerous cases which come to my attention and which I know come to the attention of other hon. members. I should like to stress something that perhaps is one of the greatest matters of urgency, apart from a change in the regulations and increases in pensions. I refer to the need to get away from something that I know must be a major concern to Members of Parliament in handling veterans problems. I refer to the fact that quite often it is necessary for a member to say he cannot do anything for a veteran because the board states that the condition is a pre-enlistment condition. If I have ever heard a hypocritical statement that is it.
When the government of Canada needed men and women to offer their lives and limbs for Canada, these men and women were examined by doctors and their cards said that they were A-l. Then, they went overseas and thousands did not return. Yet, years later when those who did return suffer from disabilities caused by their experience in war, they are turned down because of a pre-enlistment condition. Mr. Speaker, I know all of us express in our hearts the opinion that if the man has offered his life for Canada when Canada required his services, and when Canada and the government said he was A-l, no government and no country has the right years later to say he cannot receive the allowance he requires because of a pre-enlistment condition. Because of my experience over a long period in handling the cases of veterans I wanted to mention, in addition to all the other arguments, the necessity for recognition of the urgency involved before too many of our veterans pass on to the Great Beyond.
I noted with interest the remarks of previous members about Remembrance Day being two weeks away. Thousands upon thousands of people across Canada will be standing before the Cenotaphs of our country honouring the fallen. That is as it should be. But it brings to mind the statement of the men and women who offered their lives in war, "We shall not fail". The veterans of Canada, Sir, did not fail this country in time of need. I think perhaps the greatest honour we can give, not only to those who died but more specifically to those who came through and lived, is to say that by November 11 the government shall introduce all the various pieces of legislation required to meet the needs of the veterans and to bring into effect the acceptable sections of the report of the Woods commission and of the report of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. I conclude by saying, sir, the Canadian veterans did not fail us. Let us not fail them.

Veterans Allowance Increases shall). His constituency does not quickly come to mind but I heard the hon. gentleman's speech and I will remember it for a long time.
When you recognized me, Mr. Speaker you referred to me as the hon. member for Victoria. In Victoria, we have many veterans who are disabled and many of then-dependents, and the next of kin of deceased veterans. I think Victoria, in particular, has a reputation for being a city which did not spare its sons to defend what it thought was just cause, whether it was in the Boer War, in World War I and World War II or in the Korean War. Speaking personally, in my little class at school in Victoria, of the 13 pupils 12 were veterans of the second world war and the thirteenth could not be a veteran because he was serving in the U.S. merchant marine.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
When we speak of veterans pensions-and this is one of the few points that has not been brought up so far in this debate to my knowledge-many people think that all veterans receive pensions. We all know that this is not the case. We are speaking here today not of everyone who has served this country but of a special few, and of the survivors of those special few. I enjoy my work on the Veterans Affairs Committee because we help each other to help others, and surely that is what Parliament is all about. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that veterans in good health in this House and in the various veterans organizations, of which there are 11 across the country, are not trying to help themselves. We are trying to help others: the disabled, the next of kin of our war dead, and the so-called burnt-out veterans who cannot make their way in this competitive and complicated world. These are the people we are trying to help. We all do it in our own way.
I look around me and I see many of the hon. members who have already spoken on this and on the other side of the House who have helped out in special ways. The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) spoke about the Hong Kong veterans. A great number of us put in reports and recommendations to the Woods committee when it was conducting its hearings. I put forward a series of recommendations at that time, and now I would like to put in a special plug for the benefit of doubt clause to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) who just preceded me. I feel very strongly about this. I am speaking about the benefit of doubt as it relates in particular to veterans who served overseas, because as you, Mr. Speaker, know and as every other veteran knows, veterans who have served Overseas have often been denied the benefit of doubt because they have no proper medical documentation. Every veteran here will agree with me when I say that the best documented veteran is the soldier, the sailor or the airman who stayed behind in Canada. Naturally, he has the best documents because he did not have a chance to lose them anywhere. So, as I say, I would like to put in this plug for the overseas veteran who is suffering as a result of the so-called benefit of doubt clause, and I hope it is removed soon, the sooner the better.
The other day when I was at the Calgary airport I saw the now elderly and somewhat tattered Lancaster aircraft mounted outside the airport as a monument to the past. For me it was a poignant sight and it set me to thinking of our war dead, of our veterans, and of our efforts on their behalf. When I say "our efforts" I am thinking not only of the House of Commons and its Veterans Affairs Committee but also of the various veterans organizations and groups which have appeared from time to time before our committee to put forward their ideas and to give us the benefit of their advice. I had an opportunity to work closely at one time-and I am happy to say we were rewarded with some success a few years ago-with one of these groups. I am referring to the Hong Kong veterans. I will not say any more about their plight because I think much has already been said on this subject, but certainly we must not stop in our efforts to help them until every last one of them receives the minimum 48 per cent disability pension which will give protection of some sort to their wives and families.
Looking at this aircraft on the pedestal outside Calgary against the backdrop of events in Canada today, I wondered what had happened to our sense of values. We may personally and individually place the welfare of our veterans and their dependents or their next of kin high on our own scale of priorities, but this sense of values of which I speak, and its high place in our personal scale, must be reflected and incorporated in the legislation passed in this House. I can find no fault with the motion brought before the House by the hon. member for Hum-ber-St. George's-St. Barbe, and I urge the government to take speedy action to bring about a sizeable increase in both the range and the scale of benefits available to veterans and their survivors. I ask the government to go beyond the point of restoring the purchasing power of the former pensions and allowances. To my mind, those pensions and allowances were far too low, and I ask the government to remember that.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Finally, I ask the government to remember that when we enter into wars we have to realize that there is always a price to pay and it takes a long time to pay because it is a price in blood and a price in money. We are asking the government today to see to it that the nation does its duty by paying money. This is the least expensive and easiest form of payment. We should not have to wait much longer. Judging by the tone of this debate so far and by my experience with other veterans legislation that has been introduced by the government in this House, any legislation that they may care to introduce to alleviate the situation described here so eloquently today by other hon. members would, I am sure, pass very quickly. I am equally sure hon. members would delay not one whit any other government business that the government may wish to bring before the House. So my final plea, Mr. Speaker, is through you to the minister and the government to let us now get on with our job.

October 27, 1970

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-VETERANS AFFAIRS-EARLY IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AND WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I of course support the motion and I am only sorry that we have to raise this matter again. It is now 25 years since the fighting stopped in Europe, and somewhat less than that since the boys came home from Korea. But in my opinion the occurrences of the last few weeks have clearly shown that in the final analysis there is no prosperity, no freedom in a rough world except when some of our citizens pay for it with their lives, their health and their devotion. On behalf of these people who cannot be here to beg for themselves I am proud to be able to be here and beg. I am only sorry that we have to beg.
Many years ago the people of Canada, through their representatives in the House of Commons, passed the Pension Act. I believe that act is quite adequate to handle the situation. There is no necessity for a long report like the Woods committee report, which comprised some 1,300 pages in its final form, outlining in clear terms the duty of the Canadian people and of the Canadian Parliament to the people I have mentioned. Nevertheless, we now have that report. It was somewhat expensive to obtain. It is comprehensive. The Woods committee went into almost every phase of the Pension Act. As a result it has underlined what was clearly understood before its work began-that the people of Canada want to give those who have served their country so nobly and well, particularly in war, full compensation within the budget that they can meet.
The act was not foolishly generous. It only purports to give these men and their families a minimum return, which is nothing less than to put them back into civilian life as nearly as possible to the competitive position they occupied before they joined the forces. The level at which it was hoped to return them to civilian life was that of an untrained labourer. Perhaps some people would say that here is democracy working at its best. Equality was the dominant thought in the minds of the taxpayers of Canada when the Pension Act was first passed. They understood it would be administered in the fairest way possible. Section 70, which I think is the key to the whole act, stated in clear terms that the benefit of the doubt was to be given to veterans.
For reasons which the preceding speaker clearly brought out, the best soldiers, best sailors and best airmen are frequently incapable of documenting how they lost their health, unless they were wounded by gunshot, shrapnel or mine explosion to the extent that their wounds are self-evident. But it is very difficult for those who served in the front line and those who were prisoners of war to produce any document to prove that their failure in health is due to their war service.
I repeat that the people of Canada, through their members of Parliament, placed a section in the act stating that the benefit of the doubt was to be given to these men. If the benefit of the doubt had been given to them, there would be no necessity for a great deal of the Woods report. But the Hong Kong veterans had the greatest difficulty over the last 25 years even in getting a proper hearing because the people who interpreted the act asked them, "Where are your papers? Where is your medical
Veterans Allowance Increases evidence?" But, Mr. Speaker, we saw men blinded by malnutrition. We saw 190-pound men reduced to a handful of bones.
I had the privilege to help some of these people off the troopships when they came home. Their mothers did not recognize them; their wives did not recognize them. Because a third of them were blind at that time, they were not able to recognize their mothers and wives. Do you need the benefit of the doubt under conditions like that? But it has taken us 25 years of argument, hairsplitting and voluminous reports to reach the stage where we have achieved unanimous approval of measures to meet their needs.
The members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs were unanimous in the recommendations. Most of them are veterans themselves and know the story well. That committee unanimously recommended immediate action. I am very proud of the members who sat on it, from the very amiable chairman right on down through all party lines. They worked hard. They gave up several weeks of their own time to sit on the committee, to make sure that a concise and accurate report was given to the House.
But what did we get then, Mr. Speaker? We got delay. We got talk about priorities. We need no talk about priorities in this matter. Where do we put those men to whom we owe our affluent society, all the great chances we have in Canada, all the wealth we have, all the freedom we have? All we are asking is the absolute minimum required to keep them in decent clothing and shelter. The minimum pay of an untrained labourer in the public service is all we are asking for them.
The Standing Committee has given its unanimous approval. I do not know why there should be delay. I for one would be willing, without debate, to vote the necessary money. I am willing to have my income tax raised- and that is a rare concession-if that is what is holding matters up. If it is only lack of money, let us pay it. Let us borrow the money if we do not have it, and pay it to these people. I do not want to go into a long list of the frills that we have enjoyed, but I deny that there is in this case any valid argument on the necessity for weighing priorities. This matter is of the highest priority. It is a debt we all owe.
The only argument that could be advanced for not giving an increase here and now is that we do not have the money. But I do not believe that, Mr. Speaker. We cannot have it both ways. We cannot say we are one of the most prosperous young nations on earth, that we have the answers to most of our economic problems, that we have things under control, but that we cannot pay this miserable debt to the people who most need assistance.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
This is a great opportunity for our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who perhaps in the past has been misled by his own ideology or training in peacetime schools, to show us that now, in the age of his maturity he can give

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases
us the kind of leadership in peacetime that we expected in wartime for our soldiers. It is not necessary for one to be a veteran in order to reward our soldiers. The present situation gives the Prime Minister a great opportunity to show that he is now willing to stand where Canadian servicemen stood in 1939 when they faced physical danger.
If the Prime Minister has only to face political danger, I think he ought to be willing to give us leadership in this regard and to tell an unwilling cabinet and an unwilling treasury board to approve improvements in veterans legislation. I challenge him directly to say that to the cabinet. If he gives his approval to measures which will improve the lot of the veterans, I do not think many members of the cabinet, of the treasury board or those on his side of the House will oppose him. They will go along with him.
The members who served on the Veterans Affairs Committee said unanimously that these improvements are long overdue. Lest people think that I, along with the Veterans Affairs Committee, am trying to take credit for the country's awareness of the plight of the veterans, let me hasten to say that the Canadian Legion has carried on this great campaign on behalf of fallen comrades and those who have been left behind. If being turned down on many occasions could discourage some people from acting, the organization representing the Hong Kong veterans would long ago have quit trying to do something. Nevertheless, they showed the same fortitude in carrying on this campaign on behalf of their needy brethren and others as their brethren showed in the past. They made a heroic attempt to see that the right thing was done.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not say that I appreciate the effort and assistance of Dr. Richardson who brought in a magnificent report on behalf of the Hong Kong veterans. I think his report would have been unnecessary if section 70 of the act had been properly utilized. He documented the ills from which most of these boys suffered; ills such as avitaminosis, which in plain, layman's language means starving to death slowly. That magnificent report gave us an opportunity to act correctly because it brought clearly to our attention the very specific needs of this group of men.
I was greatly heartened, Mr. Speaker, when I heard that the Hong Kong veterans were to be the beneficiaries of specific legislation. We gave unanimous consent to this proposal in committee, so far as we could speak for all members of the House, and said we would not oppose the legislation in the slightest degree. Also, we gave credit to the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs and of the Department of National Health and Welfare for knowing exactly what was needed so far as veterans were concerned. We have agreed unanimously over the years that these veterans should receive special attention and that we should set aside substantial sums of money in order to help them. Their priority must be brought up to date.
In Canada we have no system of rewarding a man for valour. We invest him, when the situation merits, with a plain red ribbon. But the man who carries this plain red
ribbon-I am referring to the Victoria Cross, the highest award we can give our heroes-will no doubt say that there are many equally brave deeds which have never been recorded. I suggest that the greatest award we can give our heroes is in taking soon a new look at our veterans legislation, so that we can reward those who served so well in our time of need and look after their wives and families who, in many cases suffered even more than the soldiers who had comradeship to bolster their morale and share their burdens even unto death.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-VETERANS AFFAIRS-EARLY IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AND WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if any member of this chamber wanted to select a motion for debate to demonstrate to all Canadians that it is possible for us in the House of Commons, despite our varying orientations on many issues of policy, to attain an amazing degree of unanimity, he could have selected none better than the motion now before the House. Indeed, the motion does credit to its mover. It is one that I hasten to support.
For my part I wish to comment on a matter that has not been mentioned today in the many eloquent speeches on varying aspects of the topic before us. There is a tendency in our culture for people who are not veterans to be embarrassed when someone mentions veterans affairs. They assume that non-veterans should hold their peace and leave the discussion of veterans affairs to the "pros", to the people with actual experience. I suggest to the House that a fairly plausible argument could substantiate the opposite point of view. It is this. It seems to me that we ought to be pleased in Canada that we have not experienced a major conflict since the Korean war and that therefore we do not have a continuing supply of newly created veterans. It is a good thing not to be in the "veteran-making" business.
Secondly, it seems to me that we ought to be very pleased that our young Canadian men and women who have reached their adult years following the Second World War are willing to stand shoulder to shoulder with those who are veterans. Like others in this chamber who have spoken this afternoon, I am one of those. However, I have the good fortune to come from an area of eastern Ontario that has a large number of Legions. There are seven in my constituency. I know personally a number of veterans who keep me well informed from the "inside" point of view.
In dealing with comments that have been made in preceding speeches, I say very forcefully that I completely concur with what several speakers have said. I think the first member to mention the subject to which I am about to refer was the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae). Other hon. members also spoke on the matter. I concur in the suggestion that the Hong Kong veterans are entitled to special consideration. They have a special claim, and this fact should be reiterated in this House time and again.
The circumstances of their lives are more difficult than those of some other veterans who were treated better.
In addition, I think hon. members all know of the sense of frustration felt by families in which a veteran has

October 27, 1970

died. I refer to the sense of frustration in particular of people who have become aware, as most Canadian families which include a veteran are now aware, that we are literally on the eve of a significant overhaul of our veterans legislation. Constituents have come to me recently to express a keen sense of frustration and even bitterness about a veteran, a member of the family, who has died before this progressive step has been completed.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I assume that the reason for placing this subject before the House today is that we are so close to November 11. Approximately one year ago, on November 7, 1969, the member for York North (Mr. Danson) introduced Bill C-146, to amend the Remembrance Day Act. The gist of the bill was that the Sunday prior to November 11 would be a national day of remembrance or memorial. As the hon. member stated at that time, the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month is at present, ignored by large segments of our society and misunderstood by equally large segments.
There are two choices in this matter. One alternative is to hold the line and, in spite of the worst fears of many of us, witness the continued erosion of this very significant day of remembrance in the history of Canada and, indeed, in the history of the world. The alternative is to reorganize and restructure. I am not sure of this quotation, but I think it was Cicero who said, "He who is ignorant of what happened before he was born is destined to remain a child for ever." This quotation came to mind this afternoon when I listened to the hon. member for York-Sunbury tell the House of the incident where a group of Dutch youths tore down a wreath which had been placed on a memorial by a number of Canadian veterans. I suppose for some there is a thin line between being a warmaker or a warmonger and, on the other hand, holding in reverence the casualties of war.
The purpose of the Woods committee was to analyse the situa ion in which veterans now find themselves so that our society might better, and in very practical ways demonstrate our corporate reverence for those who paid the price and suffered the pain of war without idolizing or praising that which must be diligently avoided. We must aid war victims, not nurture reference for war. I suggest that w.e should do something-I do not pretend to have a brilliant insight into this matter-along the lines suggested by the hon. member for York North, that is, something to help our young people better appreciate the significance of Remembrance Day. We might thereby create a better mood in respect of this whole subject.
An hon. member mentioned there had been rumours that during the parades for Remembrance Day ceremonies this year some people were planning demonstrations on the assumption that those who parade on November 11 are swordrattlers, warmongers and hawks, and if you are not that kind of person you should oppose them. This is a dastardly misreading and misunderstanding of the facts. Because of this situation I again looked at the bill of the hon. member for York North. I know he was vilified by many people in our country, even by some
Veterans Allowance Increases
loyal veterans. But perhaps we could do something so that Canadians would seriously and positively appreciate what we try to do on November 11. If one had \o help war victims, without idolizing war, in the days of sword and spear, it became all the more essential in the days of bullets and bombs and a must in our day of mushrooms and missiles.
Every member of this House must, as I do, receive letters and delegations on behalf of veterans whose situations are tragic. As the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Groos) pointed out, all veterans do not automatically receive a pension. I am continually amazed at the number of Canadians who somehow assume that by virtue of being a veteran one receives a pension. People write to their Member of Parliament and ask why a certain veteran is not receiving a pension. It is obviously a widely held belief that all veterans automatically receive pensions, but as the hon. member for Victoria correctly stated, this is not true.
Obviously, for a few veterans a present situation in which they find themselves, unfortunate as it may be, cannot be linked in any direct way to war service. We are all aware of this and I need not belabor the point. However, for some there is a linkage. Therefore, time is of the essence as far as the implementation of this massive updating of our veterans legislation is concerned. When veterans die while such sweeping improvements are just around the corner, there is naturally a sense of frustration, sometimes bitter, not only by the next of kin but by all sensitive members of the House and indeed all Canadians who champion this cause.
I firmly recognize and appreciate the fact that war veterans legislation is being given proper priority by the government of Canada, especially by our distinguished Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube). I wish to read two paragraphs from the white paper on veterans pensions.
Since World War I, Canada's legislative programs for the rehabilitation and welfare of her ex-servicemen and their dependants have been recognized, internationally as well as nationally, as being broad in their scope and generous in their provisions. And this legislation has been kept flexible and dynamic; it has been amended regularly to meet the changing needs of those it serves, and to adjust it to changes in the concepts of social justice and in the Canadian economy.
Through the Pension Act, Canada endeavours to compensate as fairly as possible for the economic disadvantages caused by disability of bereavement which is related to military service. To place an accurate monetary value on human suffering and sorrow would be virtually impossible, because of the many imponderable and subjective factors involved.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-VETERANS AFFAIRS-EARLY IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AND WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have followed with interest the debate upon which the House is now engaged. I begin my contribution by saying that I fully endorse the excellent motion which has been placed before the House by my hon. friend from Humb-er-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). He is a fellow Nova Scotian who went far afield and has done well in the great province of Newfoundland. Of course, we shall always welcome him back when the time comes.
I also endorse the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Taken together, the motion and the amendment make a very forceful plea. The report of the Veterans Affairs Committee is, of course, founded upon the studies undertaken by the Woods committee; the background has been discussed in detail by other hon. members and I do not intend to repeat what they have said. Nevertheless, there are a number of aspects I wish to discuss; some of them may be called housekeeping or legal matters.
I agree with those who have said that the report which the committee made to this House and to the government was an excellent one. It covered most of the points made in the Woods committee report and set out the lines which it hoped the government would follow when introducing legislation affecting veterans. The government now has the report in its hands, and the question is: What kind of legislation will be brought in and when will it be introduced? Of course, we do not know precisely what is to be contained in the legislation and this is why we, as members of the opposition, are putting our ideas forward at this time.
There are certain provisions which I feel should be contained in any legislation to be placed before the
House. One of the recommendations contained in the report concerned the appeal procedure. As I recall the government's White Paper, it proposed the setting up of a directorate of pensions as a branch of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the effect of which would be to restrict opportunities for appeal. I trust the government will provide, in the legislation to be brought before Parliament, for a separate pension review board as recommended by the committee. This would afford veterans the opportunity, at their request, to submit pension cases for final review on the basis of a final interpretation of the act. This is most important. I can think of a number of veterans in my area and, for that matter, throughout the country who would undoubtedly have their files reopened if this course were adopted.
Another question which comes frequently to the attention of the Pension Commission and, undoubtedly, to the attention of hon. members, concerns the presumption of medical condition. This matter was referred to earlier today by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). It is possible that under the terms of the existing legislation the commission can do no other than reach the decisions it does. But since so many of these decisions are reached on the basis of a veteran's pre-enlistment medical condition, I must go along with the hon. member for Vancouver East in this respect. I trust that the legislation will deal with this question of the presumption of medical condition. The white paper, as I recall it, stated that if an adverse medical condition manifested itself within six months of a man's enlistment, it would be excluded from this presumption. The committee felt that this period should be limited to three months.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
To return to the question of the interpretation of the Pension Act, I recall sitting on several Veterans Affairs Committees and one clause that always gave us, and undoubtedly many veterans, problems was the benefit of the doubt clause. The Woods committee report proposed a completely new basis for the benefit of the doubt principle which would mean, in effect, that a pension adjudicator would be allowed to find in favour of a veteran's claim even though the veteran had not established his claim by a preponderance of evidence. In such a case the claim would be resolved in favour of the veteran rather than the government through its Department of Veterans Affairs.
To be fair to the government, the white paper recognized the problems that have arisen over the interpretion of this section of the act and proposed the rewriting of the section to incorporate guidelines in regard to what constituted the benefit of the doubt. Although I hope this proposal will be taken up, I contend the benefit of the doubt principle should be applied in favour of the veteran, not in favour of the government. A veteran should not have to prove his case by a preponderance of evidence.
I have also had quite a bit to do with veterans bureaux in the Atlantic area as well as in Ottawa, and I have nothing but praise for them. It has been suggested that the veterans bureaux are serving two masters, and I do

October 27, 1970

not think that this should be the case. I would support the conclusion agreed upon by the parliamentary committee and proposed by the Woods committee that the veterans bureaux should be established under a separate part of the Pension Act so they can report directly to the minister. They should be cast in the role of acting strictly as the applicant's advocate and should be relieved of the responsibility of reporting unfavourable evidence to the commission. Such a recommendation was endorsed in the government's white paper and supported by the parliamentary committee of which I was a member.
I have several files in my office in connection with members of the regular forces who have been injured while on duty. According to the relevant section of the act, members of the regular forces must show that any injuries were sustained in the course of duty. Sometimes this is quite difficult to prove. In some instances, where there was an irregularity, it has been held they were not acting in the course of their duty. For example, I recall a case concerning a young airman who was walking across an air base in this country, against a red traffic light, en route to the control tower when he was knocked down by a civilian vehicle. The commission did not rule whether he was injured in the course of his duty, but held that since he was guilty of contributory negligence at the time, he was not entitled to a pension. There is no provision in the act to deal with this situation.
The committee was of the view that the act should be revised to provide presumptions upon which a pension could be approved where death or disability had arisen from physical training, sport activity, transportation and other acts done as part of service operations, training or administration. I hope that this point will be covered by the minister and will be included in the legislation to come before the House.
Other hon. members have spoken about the burnt-out pension under the War Veterans Allowance Act. I have many files in my office on this issue. It has already been pointed out that the present allowance is $1,260 for a single person and $2,100 for a married person, both figures being below what we have called the 1968 poverty line of $1,800 and $3,000 for a single and a married person respectively.
I also want to raise the question of permissible income, which is better known as the income ceiling. I think this ceiling should be raised. At the present time, to be eligible under the legislation the combination of other income and the allowance that a veteran receives must not exceed, if he is a single man, $1,740 a year or, if he is a married man, $2,940 a year-still below the poverty line. I suggest the income, including the war veterans allowance, the burnt-out pension, should be at least $2,280 for a single person and $3,840 for a married person.
Not long after the guaranteed income supplement legislation was passed, I met a veteran on the street in my home town who told me he had applied for the GIS because he was told it would not affect his war veterans allowance. However, his war veterans allowance was cut and he found himself worse off, financially, than he was before he applied for the GIS. I fail to see any equity in
Veterans Allowance Increases this situation. I contend that payments like the guaranteed income supplement, old age security and so on, should not be considered income and included in the income ceiling prescribed by the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I have taken enough time in this debate, Mr. Speaker. I fully endorse the matters that have been put before the House by the committee. As I said when I commenced my speech, the question is: When will the government bring in the new legislation? I say the sooner, the better. I hope the legislation will contain the most important of the points that I have put before the House this evening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could summarize the measures our country has taken since World War II to show its gratitude, but I shall only mention the program for rehabilitation to civilian life, education assistance to veterans, assistance programs for the children of war dead, measures to help veterans settle on farms and housing assistance. I cannot keep on like this, although I would like to do so, because in all fairness, we must recognize that all Canadian governments have acted decently with respect to war veterans.
Last May, I had the opportunity and the privilege and the honour of heading a delegation of veterans who went to Holland to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the liberation of the Dutch people. It should be recalled that Holland was liberated by Canadian troops. Actually, this is the only country in the world ever to be liberated by Canadian forces. During the ceremonies, I had a chat with Prince Bernhardt and among other things I told him about my duties as Minister of Veterans Affairs and about the activities of my department. His Royal Highness was amazed at the efforts made by the Canadian government for the well-being of its war veterans. Indeed, I know of only one other minister responsible for

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases
war veterans apart from me, and it is my French counterpart. Our allies, the United States and Great Britain have decided after a period of 25 years that having such a department was no longer justifiable. We have continued to do so and I am pleased to announce to the House that next week, I will have the opportunity to go to France, to revive our common memories, to renew our good relations with that country, to meet my opposite number the French Minister of Veterans Affairs, and to visit Vimy and Beaumont-Hamel as a representative of the Canadian government before those great monuments which are the symbol not only of glorious wartime feats, but also of the many Canadians who gave up their lives or in certain cases their limbs or their health.
But the members of the Canadian government, Mr. Speaker, do more than stand at attention in front of monuments-
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)

What we are trying to do is not only to stand at attention before monuments, but we do remember veterans and we are continuing year after year trying to give them the best possible services available in Canada. These services will cost Canadian taxpayers this year $500 million-half a billion dollars which we are dispensing for our veterans. We are trying to do this in a very efficient manner so as not to spend uselessly the taxpayers' money. I am sure that no Canadian will ever reproach us for giving that much attention and that much financial assistance to our veterans. I know that all hon. members, especially from what I have heard this afternoon, want us to do even more. They can rest assured that the points they have made this afternoon with reference to disability pensions and war veterans allowances have been well noted.
Of course, it is not my place to make an announcement now, but I can assure the House that this government, as all Canadian governments have in the past, will do its utmost for our veterans. Before we talk about increases I should state-perhaps the public does not know this- that at the present time a Canadian veteran with a family of five receives in disability pension the sum of $5,496 a year, tax free. I am very pleased about that and I say it with joy. Of course, we intend to do more. Some hon. members who spoke this afternoon claimed that veterans were living in dire poverty. With regard to war veterans allowances, they were increased in 1965 and again in 1966. We know of course, that the cost of living has gone up; we are not blind to that situation.
Most of the members who spoke this afternoon stressed the urgency of passing legislation in this field and said we were not moving fast enough. I would agree with them. I would be the happiest man in this House if all my problems were solved in one day-but this is not how democracy works. If the wheels of justice are slow, the wheels of Parliament are even slower. This legislation is not being delayed by me.
Perhaps I should state a few facts. It took two years for the Woods committee report to be presented. It is a good
report which contains 148 recommendations. The House of Commons Committee on Veterans Affairs sat for ten months. I should compliment that committee and its chairman. The members took time off from their holidays and away from their families and businesses to come here and work on behalf of the veterans of this country, with no extra pay. During that time they heard a number of witnesses-I do not know how many-from veterans associations who appeared on 19 occasions; they received 19 briefs. The committee studied those briefs and produced a report. I received that report only the day before this House adjourned for the summer recess. During the summer recess the report was brought before the appropriate cabinet committee, at which time decisions were taken. The whole matter now is being sent to the Department of Justice for the purpose of producing legislation. I am confident that the legislation will be introduced in the very early part of this session.
This all took a long time, I agree, but it was not delayed by me or by anyone in the House. This is the normal process of legislation; it does take time. When the legislation is introduced, I think all members of this House will find that it was well worth waiting for, because it will be good legislation; it will be advanced legislation, modern, generous and very humane.
We have been talking all afternoon about veterans. I am not a veteran; I was only 12 when the war was declared. People do not seem to realize that 50 per cent of the population of Canada today is under the age of 25. There is what you might call a generation gap or a memory gap. If there is a generation gap between two generations, I think the large portion of the burden of bridging that gap is not on the younger generation but, rather, on us. We are the ones who created the world in which they live. They were not even witness to the events that shaped our times.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I think that veterans and veterans associations, which are very well structured across the country with Legions in almost every small town, have a role to play and are equipped to play it well. They must explain to the young people what they themselves did 25 years ago to preserve the freedom of the world, its unity and the unity of this country. I believe the veterans of this country now have a very strong role to play in our unity. They may be called upon to fight again, not with guns and bayonets but with the moral fibre of their courage and with dignity because of the respect and appreciation they receive from the people surrounding them. They should use that quality to again help the government and the members of this House to cement unity in this country.
When they fought 25 years ago they cared not whether the comrade next to them was from Manitoba, Quebec or New Brunswick; they fought together for principles in which they believed very dearly. They came back here and there was no war outside the country to which they would be sent. There is no war in this country now, but there is no doubt there is a struggle in which they can help and make a contribution because of their experience

October 27, 1970

and the appreciation they have acquired from their fellow citizens.

Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I shall thank again those who have taken part in this debate. I am most satisfied to realize once again that they have put veterans affairs above party politics, and that we are all convinced of the need to do more for those who have fought to preserve democracy and our freedom. I fully agree with them and I wish to give myself entirely to this cause. I have the feeling that, in a short while, all veterans will be most satisfied with the government's attitude towards them.

I am also very conscious of the fact that I have a responsibility to represent in this House the veterans who live in my constituency, in my province, and indeed all the veterans of Canada. We all have this responsibility. I am particularly conscious of the contribution the veterans are making to my own province and to my own constituency, just as I am deeply conscious of the contribution they made to preserve the very society they are now helping to sustain.
Perhaps we should reflect for a moment upon the wording of the motion. It is a very simple motion. It is a motion calling upon the government to do two things. First of all, it calls upon the government to implement a

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases unanimous recommendation of one of the Standing Committees of this House, a recommendation contained in the second report of the Committee on Veterans Affairs, dated June 9, 1970. Second, it calls upon the government, in addition to proceeding with the implementation of these recommendations, to provide adequate increases in the allowances paid under the War Veterans Allowance Act of 1952.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
I think it is only fair that we should ask ourselves why it is necessary to proceed in this manner; why we find it necessary to bring in a motion calling upon the government to implement the unanimous recommendations of one of the Standing Committees of this House, recommendations resulting from a study referred to the committee by the House, by the government itself.
The minister has referred to the outstanding work of the Veterans Affairs Committee, as have other hon. members, the endless hearings, the briefs, the hearings of witnesses, the examination of the government White Paper and the examination of the Woods report. All of this was done in a period of 10 months, and in many instances at times when Parliament was in recess.
I find it exceedingly difficult to understand why the government has not acted upon the unanimous recommendations of this committee, especially in light, notwithstanding what the minister has said, of the circumstances of which most hon. members are aware-of the sufferings of many of our veterans today who are operating under great hardship because of the consequences of inflation and the spiralling cost of living that has reduced their incomes under the War Veterans Allowance Act, as well as their pensions, to the point where they have to endure great hardships.
Many veterans unable to continue to work or to find work are forced to fall back on the government and depend upon the War Veterans Allowance Act to sustain themselves. But I ask the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, how much sustenance can a married man with dependents purchase on $175 a month, which is the maximum payable under the act even with the maximum supplementary earnings of $245 that he is entitled to have.
I ask the minister, as a family man who knows what it is to support a family, to put himself in the position of having to feed his wife and his children on $60 a week, because that is what we are asking the veterans of this country to do by maintaining the present level under the War Veterans Allowance Act. How can any Canadian expect to maintain his dignity while living on such a pittance?
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that those who are unfortunate enough to have to fall back on the War Veterans Allowance Act are being denied the dignity that should be theirs by right and by virtue of the contribution and the sacrifice they have made. Yet we are reducing them to a bare sustenance. The minister, the government, and indeed all of us should hang our heads in shame because I think it is a shame in this affluent
country of ours that we should bring our veterans, who have paid such a price to sustain this country, to such a pitiful state.
We do not even pay any attention to the poverty level set down by the Economic Council of Canada in 1968. Indeed, sir, we pay our veterans less than the very minimum wage laws enacted by this Parliament. Yet the veterans of Canada have to sustain themselves with the knowledge that any promise of an increase in their allowances will only come after a review of the whole social legislation on the statute books of Canada. I hope the minister will pay heed to the pleading of members in this debate. I hope he will live up to the responsibility that is his as Minister of Veterans Affairs and that he will recognize the plight of the veterans.
I reject the view that has aready been reiterated by the minister in the speech he made tonight, subtle though it may be, that veterans allowances should somehow be lost in the general review of social legislation. I say this because when the Parliament of Canada established the very department over which the minister now has the responsibility of presiding, and when Parliament enacted the legislation on the statute books of this country to deal with the problems of veterans and to recognize the role that our veterans have played in maintaining the society we enjoy, Parliament was paying particular attention to the obligation of the whole country to our veterans. Parliament was not suggesting that we should provide for the veterans in the same context that we provide for the unemployed, for the socially indigent or for the handicapped. Parliament was recognizing the special and unique obligation that this country has to those who served Canada in war.
I believe that we are reaching the stage where we are trying to get out from under that obligation, and I think it is a bad thing for Canada. This Parliament has recognized its obligations to those in the country who have to fall back upon the protection of the minimum wage laws. It has recognized the spiralling cost of living in this country, and in so doing has said that by law no one in Canada who is within the jurisdiction of the federal government shall receive less than $1.65 an hour. Surely the government has the same obligation to the veterans of this country, recognizing the same factors that are driving up the cost of living and are depriving veterans of their income. Surely the government must recognize the toll that inflation has taken upon war veterans allowances and upon disability pensions, and should act very quickly.
Not a month has gone by since the outset of this Parliament in 1968 without my receiving an inquiry from a veteran in my constituency asking when the government is going to act upon the Woods report. Barely a month goes by without my having to explain to the veterans why the government has refused to act. It is an empty explanation and one that I could not accept; consequently, I cannot expect veterans in my constituency and in my province to accept it.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-VETERANS AFFAIRS-EARLY IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AND WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commence my remarks by congratulating the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for introducing this motion, and by congratulating the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Veterans Allowance Increases Knowles) for the excellent and pointed amendment he made to it.
Following the Second World War there was a mood in this country in which people were determined to see that veterans, those who had fought on behalf of the nation, on behalf of the liberties we all hold so dear, would be given a fair portion of the rewards that society had to offer, and that justice would be given them in terms of opportunities and as a reward for their service. For a considerable period following the end of the war we maintained this objective in a very strong way. However, as the years went by, as the war faded into memory and as the sacrifices of the men and women who participated in that war faded into memory, it seems that government interest in the veterans took a less urgent turn.
We had all hoped that the minister would rise today and give us some specific and encouraging information on the government's approach to changes in veterans legislation. The minister had an opportunity to speak for half an hour and he made a statement. He said all the right things but, when it was all over, the minister had said nothing. That was a very great disappointment to all of us.
Because of my high regard for the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube) I am prepared to accept his statement that he would like to implement the very good recommendations of the Veterans Affairs Committee. I think he is saying this with all sincerity. But if the minister feels this way, why is the legislation not before the House, or at least legislation incorporating some of the things on which we have all agreed? If the fault does not lie with the minister, surely there is an area in which it does lie, an area that has to be criticized sharply by this House. Who is responsible? The government has the power; it has the means at its disposal. We can only assume that the minister is not the only one who is holding up the legislation, and that the government has very little inclination to introduce veterans legislation. That is a sad conclusion to reach.
It must be obvious to all hon. members that, when it wants, a government can take quick action. I would like to point out some of the quick actions this government has taken. Let us take an instance in connection with the white paper on tax reform, where we had what was supposed to be a total package, somewhat analogous to the situation with respect to the recommendations of the Veterans Affairs Committee. For a long time the government took the position that no part of the white paper could be modified or changed until the finance committee had met, had made its recommendations and the government had had an opportunity to review those recommendations.
However, on a number of occasions while that committee was still sitting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) announced very great changes in the white paper proposals, particularly with regard to the natural resource industry and more particularly with regard to the mining industry. Does this mean that mining interests in Canada have more say with, more pull over, and more

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases
influence on the government than do the nation's veterans? That would certainly appear to be the case.
I give another example of government action. Recently the government felt compelled to introduce the War Measures Act. At the time it was introduced many hon. members insisted that the act be limited in time and that the government come to the House and introduce more specific and better legislation to deal with the events that had occurred. The government was able to promise that within 30 days it would bring legislation before the House. This is not uncomplicated legislation; I am talking about some very profound changes in the laws of the country. I am glad the government felt able to suggest it could do this within 30 days.
But surely after examination given by the Veterans Affairs Committee to the recommendations of the Woods committee, the government is in a much better position to draft new veterans legislation and put it before the House? I cannot find any possible excuse for the government's delay in changing existing veterans legislation to improve the conditions of many of the men and women who willingly offered themselves in the service of the nation.
It is an unfortunate truth that the government has not placed any urgency on this matter. One suspects that, very much like its attitude toward old age pensioners, the veterans are part of the government's fight against inflation; that the veterans, like the old age pensioners, are being held as hostages in the government's fight against inflation, a fight that it cannot win and a fight that is unjust beyond belief.
Earlier, my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre made a most eloquent and, as always, reasonable plea on behalf of the veterans. My hon. friend has on many occasions risen in this House on behalf of those who need the help of our nation. One wonders if, while he was speaking for those veterans, he did not have in mind a broader problem. It is interesting, when one looks back at the history of our treatment of veterans, to realize that when we helped the veterans of Canada we were also helping all people in this country. When we brought in social justice for our veterans we also extended it to other people in our society.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
What we have done for veterans has often pioneered what we have done in social change. We have adopted attitudes that tended to improve the lot of the Canadian people. For example, let me point out one very important area which we could consider-the area of education. We forget that before 1945 and 1946 little assistance was given to people who wanted to go on to higher education. The idea of providing loans or grants for education was not in common currency at that time. Loans were introduced for veterans of the armed forces, and they were able to avail themselves of university educations. From there on society progressively extended help to others, and this turned out to be a most admirable approach which helped other people in society to obtain an education. Much of the vocational training program we have
today has resulted from concepts and policies developed after the end of the war.
Also, let us look back on the Veterans' Land Act. This is one of the first instances in which the government became involved in publicly assisted housing. It is most unfortunate it did not do more of this. Nevertheless, thousands of veterans in this country today would not have homes if they had not been assisted under the Veterans' Land Act. That legislation has changed our concept about the public's involvement in housing. Although we have not gone as far as I should like to see us go, at least that legislation changed some of the attitudes and some of the directions in which this country was going.
When we consider the burnt-out pension and the war veterans allowance, we see the beginning of the concept of a guaranteed income. Indeed, programs that were begun for veterans have often been extended to other areas of our society. I make these points to show why I think it is important for us to support the idea of veterans benefits both for those who are veterans and for those who are not. I say this regardless of the justice of the situation. This country owes an elementary obligation to those people who served in its armed forces. There is the added point that, as I have said, what we do for our veterans today we often will do for other people tomorrow, and veterans legislation is an important indicator of social attitudes.

Therefore, I cannot accept the arguments presented tonight by the minister. I cannot accept his reasons for delay. We are not delaying because we are so poor in this country that we can do nothing; neither are we delaying because the machinery of government is so creaky that nothing can be done. The machinery is creaky only when the government wants it to be creaky. It acts very quickly in the middle of the night when the government wants it to work that way.
I think members on all sides of the House markedly agree that there has been much too much delay in improving the lot of veterans in Canada, and that this should be corrected as quickly as possible. I was glad to hear that the minister intended making a trip to Europe in order to visit some of the monuments and pay his respect to the brave men and women who died for their country. I suggest to the minister that he could do no better in paying his respect to those brave men and women than by moving quickly and bringing in increased and much needed benefits for those veterans who are still living.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assure the hon. member who rose at the same time I did that I will stay and listen to his speech. I know that he has a good deal to offer the House and I would not miss his remarks for the world. I will not take too long in what I am about to say because, quite frankly, I believe everyone who has spoken this afternoon and evening is in agreement about

October 27, 1970

what should be done and there is no necessity for my talking at length.
My reason for rising tonight is that I feel, as a member of the Veterans Affairs Committee of the House of Commons, that I am under an obligation to say a few words. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-VETERANS AFFAIRS-EARLY IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AND WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) did such an excellent job in outlining the position of the official opposition on matters dealing with veterans, in his extremely able and comprehensive speech, that it is not necessary for me to deal with the points he made. However, for a very few moments I would like to deal with the treatment this government gives veterans who receive the war veterans allowance.
I have three very strong objections to the treatment which the government is meting out to these very deserving veterans. The first is that this government has not seen fit to increase the war veterans allowance since 1966, despite the fact that during the four years since then the cost of living has increased by nearly 20 per cent. Several times each year the opposition has pressed the government strongly to increase the war veterans allowance proportionately with the cost of living. By not increasing the war veterans allowance during the past four years, the government has simply said to the veteran, "Tighten your belt. Do without more and more of the things that you need to keep body and soul together for you and your family".
I believe this is just the reverse of the way that members of the armed forces in World War I and World War
II	should be treated. By giving so much they literally burned themselves out during their war service. They need our assistance in civilian life. That is my first reason for strongly condemning the attitude of this government toward those receiving war veterans allowance.
My second point is that the government prohibits a single man earning more than $40 a month, or $70 a month for a married man over and above the war veterans allowance which he receives. These war veterans allowances are an absolute minimum. It is well recognized that no one could even come close to maintaining themselves on such a small pension. They are simply assistance. If a man wishes to improve the standard of living for himself and his family and works hard to earn
money to supplement the allowance, that is to be admired. To allow these veterans to earn only $40 a month or $70 a month restricts very greatly their ability to maintain a decent standard of living and support their families in the way they would wish and have every right to do, particularly in view of the great service they have performed for their country.
The attitude of the government in this regard discourages initiative. It discourages a man's desire to earn as much as he can to improve the financial position of his family. I am sure all members of the House have felt that this restriction is very unfair. It should be cancelled. A man receiving war veterans allowance should be permitted to earn as much as he can by working.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The other matter to which I object very strongly is the way in which the government treats those members of the armed forces who not only receive the veterans allowance but also the old age pension. As we all know, when the old age pension is increased, as it is occasionally by even this parsimonious government, it is increased for a very good reason; it is increased because the cost of living has gone up and because the government rightly considers that those receiving the old age pension need considerably more to live on. But if a man is receiving both the old age pension and the veterans allowance, any increase in the old age pension is deducted from what he receives by way of veterans allowance. Thus, though the cost of living has increased and pensioners are getting an increase in their pension, the man who is also receiving veterans allowance gets no increase at all.
I ask those who are seated on the treasury benches tonight whether they consider that this is fair treatment of our veterans. There is silence from the treasury benches because their occupants are obviously ashamed of what the government has done in the past few years. They realize it is a disgraceful way to treat those who have served their country so well. It is high time the minister and his colleagues corrected this miscarriage of justice and allowed pensions and war veterans allowances to be increased independently of each other. When an increase in either is brought before Parliament and passed, it should be allowed in full to those pensioners who are receiving veterans allowances, because they have served their country well. Judging by the way in which the government treats those who receive veterans allowances-that is to say in a penny-pinching, miserly and completely unjustified manner-we shall have to press our case very hard if we wish to succeed.
This penny-pinching on the part of the government is in strange contrast with its actions when it comes to buying airplanes of which it has no need. It has been brought to the attention of the House and of the country that four years ago the government ordered $250 million worth of CF-5 planes to enable the armed forces of this country to play a peacekeeping role as part of the United Nations peacekeeping efforts. Two years ago, in 1968, this peacekeeping role was abandoned. But instead of cancelling the order for these planes, because they happened to

be produced in the Prime Minister's home riding in Montreal-this can be the only reason-the decision was made to keep the aircraft rolling off the assembly lines though there is not the slightest need for them in our air force. Some of them have even been sent to Europe as a public relations gesture to find out whether they could be of use there. They could not.

speechtext:
Listening to this debate, Mr. Speaker, I would imagine that throughout the centuries every government has been faced with the same dilemma-every kingdom, every principality, every parliament and every minister. It is not a new story. It is said by Arrian in his record of the wars of Alexander, in his history giving an account of the anabasis, that when the great Macedonian warrior addressed his troops just before they returned home, he told them "I have provided for you and I have set up statues to those who have fallen; I have provided you with gold plate from the loot of Syria, India and Cathay." And all those things he did. But the historian went on to say that when the troops returned home they found the gold had disappeared and most of them lived thereafter in abject poverty.
Napoleon's armies fared no better, nor did the armies of Wellington. But these were old days. When we speak of those days we are talking about rewards, we are talking about some sort of compensation. This is not the issue here at all. The hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) says there is some deep, dark plot on the part of the minister to use veterans pensions in the govern-
Veterans Allowance Increases ment's fight against inflation. That is utter nonsense; it is not the case at all.
I compliment the minister for having stayed here throughout this debate, as he should have done. We are dealing with a million people and with a question which calls for a revision of our thinking, one which calls for a new look. I must say I cannot agree at all with the Woods committee report. The trouble is that commissions, instead of taking a brand new approach to a problem, always get together and say: Let us take a look at the existing legislation. Then on the basis of the status quo they amend, they split hairs, and no new approach is ever taken.
So it is here. We have listened to speeches in this House today in the course of which members have stated they begged the government to show consideration. How dare they beg on behalf of the veterans? Who gave them a mandate to beg? When you beg, you lower a man's dignity. Nobody gave them the right to beg, and the veterans do not want them, or any hon. member, to beg the minister for anything. The veterans gave no mandate to anyone to go around with a cup for alms. This is not the issue. This is where we have gone astray, although it seems that year after year someone feels compelled to beg the government for more money. Where does one get this right? Who gave them this right? This is not a begging situation. What the veterans want is equity, not alms, not some consideration in return for having fought.
It is surprising that after the war the Liberal government took the correct attitude when it undertook to provide veterans with opportunities to go to university, to get an education, to get adequate housing, and so on. This was not a response to begging; it was not a reward for having fought. The whole principle was based upon the fact that veterans had lost time. They might have stayed here and worked and prepared themselves for university, acquired funds, a house, a car and furniture.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The compensation was this: the government recognized that they had contributed to the security of our country and, accordingly, assisted them to place themselves in a position of equality as compared with those who were not members of the armed services. That was the whole point. But when it came to pensions, the government reverted to the age old idiom of gifts. Why did they not go a little further? Why the principle of the unskilled labourer? Is there a presumption that the average veteran would not have been more successful? No, there is not. Yet this provision was passed in 1918 and has been favoured by commission after commission because it was so much easier to continue the same amount in effect than to bend some effort to make a change.
The maximum amount should be the average amount earned by all working veterans. That is the amount that would be equitable. I hope the minister is listening, because this would provide a wonderful opportunity for the government to introduce the concept of a guaranteed annual income. Here is a group asking to be given the

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases
opportunity to be placed on the same level as other people. It is a controlled group. Nobody would dare suggest that our veterans would abuse the guaranteed annual income, because they would not be veterans if they did.
Implementation of this idea would dispense with appeal boards, various pension schemes, the onus of proof now placed on veterans, and so on. After all, who can say what in a service-connected injury? I dare anyone to define that expression. Who can judge what is going to be the reaction of a man who lives under constant stress for four or five months of the year? And in the field one is under constant stress. If medical opinion is correct, no one can predict the consequences to a man's health of a life under stress. Frustration, enforced discipline and things of that nature must have an effect on the health of a man. As a result, no one can define what is and what is not a service-connected injury.
Recently I had occasion to plead the case of a man suffering from lung cancer. It is recognized today that the inhalation of smoke affects the lungs. This man was in the REME. I know from personal experience that in these field operation units the men are working under cover since often it is cold, and exhaust fumes from vehicles are constantly being pumped into the air. For five years this man lived in an environment of pollution. Yet the board held that there was no proof his lung cancer had any connection with his service.
The guaranteed annual income would be the answer in such a case. Those who did not need the guaranteed annual income would not take it. Many of those in receipt of disability pension would be only too happy to give it up. After all, the very system we have been fighting for does enable us to make a living and to make our way in the world. As I say, if the guaranteed annual income for veterans is accepted by the government, it will not cost more money. In addition, it will dispense with all appeals, pension boards and eliminate the sort of friction that has been the experience to date.
It was said today that our veterans should be given more money as a reward for valour. Valour, Mr. Speaker, is not rewarded. No man who is courageous or valorous expects reward; he is courageous or valorous because he loves his country. He knew that on occasion he would have to shed blood and tears if he loved his country, and this is still being done to this day. So you do not reward valour.

I did not notice many of the members who were here earlier. I was here because I wanted to catch Your Honour's eye. I am not a veteran, and I speak because I am not a veteran. I was too young to serve. I found the veterans in this House this afternoon trying, as I did, to be recognized. I want to say two or three serious things. This afternoon I listened to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), who is sitting in his seat tonight as he has sat attentively all during this debate. As the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) said earlier, as well as the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. McBride), I do not think any topic that has come to the floor of this House has been received with such unanimity as this one. In fact, I can stand here tonight and say that I do not know of a member in this House who represents more veterans or more legionaires than I do in my riding of Annapolis Valley. I know for a fact from my predecessor in that constituency that more veterans came to his office than to the offices of all the other members from Nova Scotia combined. I have inherited part of that legacy and part of that challenge. Perhaps I am not as capable of dealing with this matter as my predecessors seat were. For that reason, and because of the historic interest in veterans and veterans' problems, I want to say a few words. Believe me, they will be very few.
Veterans Allowance Increases I listened to the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe and to the hon. member for Ottawa West make very constructive contributions to this debate. Many of the members who followed them were members of the Veterans Affairs Committee. I was struck by one consistent current that flowed throughout their contributions, namely, that this was a non-partisan committee.
