speechtext:
I do not know who said, "Come on, Pat" but I will come on to him any time he wants me to if he will stand up and identify himself. How many of those veterans contributed their efforts to the wars of this country with a non-partisan spirit and heart? Do not get me wrong; I am not talking about partisanship in the sense of whether you belong to the great Liberal party, the great Conservative party, the great NDP or the great Creditiste party. I ask in all seriousness, through you, Mr. Speaker, whether anyone knows of a veteran who has come to him for assistance with a vacant heart, a vacant mind, a vacant soul or a vacant spine. They are not non-partisan. This clap-trap about non-partisanship is a lot of idiocy.
Who knows more about partisanship than those who contributed their full effort to the war? I say in all sincerity through you, Mr. Speaker, to the members of the Veterans Affairs Committee and to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube), whom I respect as a man who has no peer in this House as far as sincerity is concerned, that the veterans of this country are not interested in the non-partisan aspect of this House.
The motion advanced by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe was designed to benefit the veterans of this country. I have in mind all those veterans who read this report, who read Hansard or sit in the galleries listening to our debates. There are never many in the gallery, because they do not want to hear about the non-partisan character of this committee or of the House of Commons. They know what their partisanship was during the war. They know where their spirits were, where their hearts were. Some of them know where their limbs are now, and some of them who are not here tonight know where their souls rest.
I suggest to you and through you, Mr. Speaker, to the members of the Veterans Affairs Committee and to the minister that we should get away from these pious platitudes about non-partisanship. Let us not waste words about whether we were partisan. Let us do as the Veter-

ans Affairs Committee did in its unanimous report, that is, become completely partisan toward the cause of veterans. That is the type of partisanship that should not take second place to any feeling in this House. That is what is lost when speaker after speaker today stood up and talked almost exclusively for five or ten minutes about the committee being non-partisan.
This House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada has put into effect the best pension plan known to man. We were non-partisan in that regard. Do we think that the veteran who wants an adjustment in his pension, or the pension of a widow or child who is dependent upon war veterans allowance, cares about whether we are Liberals, Conservatives or members of the NDP as far as partisanship is concerned? This is just flying a false flag. We are going to flounder in the swampland unless we start to accept reality and appreciate it.
I wanted to contribute to this debate because the people who fought for the rights of this institution and the freedom of speech about which we talk are the very people who will become disillusioned if this Parliament of Canada does not during this session do something concrete about veterans' problems. We must do something for them through the pension plan, war veterans allowances or the Canadian Pension Commission. This commission has worked unceasingly for veterans. It is because I feel very strongly, even as a non-veteran, that I make these suggestions.

I listened to the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) earlier this afternoon. He recited the pages of history that I used to read. He spoke about the battles he fought, about which I have read. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as recorded at page 425 of the official report of the House of Commons' debates for October 22, 1970, I asked the Minister of National Health
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion and Welfare (Mr. Munro) a question which reads in part as follows:
Yesterday, the Department of National Health and Welfare published a report which says that the cost of hospital, medical and dental care has almost quadrupled in Canada between 1957 and 1969. Here is my question: Is the department now considering measures-
-to prevent the quadrupling of these costs again between 1970 and 1980 without improvement in services, or to have hospital and medical services made more accessible to the people?
In the course of my brief remarks tonight, Mr. Speaker, I would like to prove, with the help of statistics, that the erroneous policy of nationalizing medical services through Medicare was a piece of bluff and has misled the people.
The figures are as follows: In 1957, we spent $1 billion for various medical services. In 1969, these expenses rose to $3.9 billion. As for the area of personal health care, these expenses rose from $600 million in 1957 to $2.5 billion in 1969. Medical care amounted to $272 million in 1957 and to $910 million in 1969. However, between 1968 and 1969, that is to say after the introduction of the famous hospital insurance plan in some provinces, the cost for these items increased by $122 million. Moreover, the cost of drugs was $103 million in 1957 and $270 million in 1969.
In the light of these figures, we have the right to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare what steps he intends to take in order to stop this escalation.
Mr. Speaker, if the present situation is allowed to go on, within a few years, medical costs will be beyond the reach of everybody or will take up the greater part of the provincial budgets. The population will not enjoy more services and only confusion will follow.
Almost all provincial governments have been compelled to set up medicare and without being a prophet of doom I think that before five years, in Quebec, we shall go through a recession.
There were still in Quebec-I admit it-under the former medical set up, numerous hospitals that might have been called infirmaries. But, instead of coming to the help of the medical and health services by improving what needed improvement, the federal governement levied taxes on the provinces and then forced them to establish a medical care plan if they wanted to be entitled to a reimbursement of the taxes levied for that purpose. That was the "believe or die" policy and, very soon, it will be responsible for the crisis in which the provinces will find themselves.
Because of the false socialistic principle of state mede-cine advocated by the present government, the following consequences will be felt: Firstly, incompetence will appear at all levels of medical practice; secondly, the real desire of attending the sick that the doctors used to have will disappear; thirdly, the costs of state medicine paid by the government but squeezed out of the taxpayer will become prohibitive; fourthly, we will see mediocrity at all levels of the medical profession; and finally the dying will await death in hospital corridors without getting first

aid, while people with imaginary diseases will fill the hospital beds which should be reserved to the sick.
Medicine will have lost its noble characteristics because instead of providing services to the individual and allowing him to choose his physician, his hospital and all other services, the state will have previously stripped the individual of his purchasing power before controlling medicine and establishing a barrier of redtape between the medical profession and the patients, making everyone dissatisfied, doctors and patients alike.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply tonight to the grievance voiced by the hon. member from Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), and I should like to thank him by the same token for his most emotional speech in this respect.
I would like to remind him that in November 1968, the Minister of National Health and Welfare convened an interprovincial conference of health ministers to consider the problem of the ever rising cost of medical care.
Following this conference, a study group was appointed whose report, in three volumes, was introduced in the House last November. As a result of this, a task force was appointed to implement the recommendations contained in this first report. Some recommendations, by the way, have already been implemented by provincial governments.
Finally, the last group was asked to make recommendations to be considered at the next federal-provincial conference of health ministers to be held in December.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of hon. members on some aspects of this fundamental problem.
The main reason for greater costs is the spiralling increase in wages which represent from 70 to 80 per cent of the total cost of health care in Canada. In my opinion, this is a very serious problem. We must also consider that the care provided is of a higher standard, that better prophylaxis prevents epidemics and reduces infant mortality.
Besides, physicians, nurses and health technicians are getting more advanced and more general training. The range of diagnostic tests, medication and highly specialized equipment is forever increasing.
This general expansion, which is part of the quality of care, certainly represents another major factor in the spiralling increase of health care costs in Canada.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, these are only a few examples and reality is infinitely more complex.
In any case, the members know very well that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has long realised the existence of this thorny issue and that he has taken every possible measure to solve it. The federal government and the provinces are fully aware that there is a very serious financial problem, and I can say that all levels of government are prepared to co-operate in order to remedy this unfortunate situation.

NATIONAL DEFENCE-RECONSIDERATION OF CLOSING OF RIVERS AIR BASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 23 I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald, Rosedale) the following question as reported on page 513 of Hansard:
Has the decision to close the Canadian Armed Forces base at Rivers, Manitoba, been reconsidered, since it is the only suitable airfield available for transporting troops in any emergency from Camp Shilo, as was shown by the extreme difficulties experienced last week in the enforced reactivating of Rivers in order to move troops to Montreal?
The minister's reply was:
Mr. Speaker, these facts were very much taken into account when the earlier decisions were arrived at but there has been no reconsideration since the event the hon. member was referred to.
The reason, Mr. Speaker, I have brought this matter up on the adjournment debate is that the people of Rivers and the people of Western Manitoba deserve a better answer than the minister gave. In fact, there are many questions pertaining to Rivers Air Base that this government has never answered or explained. I want to state that if the government can save tax dollars by closing surplus military bases, I agree with them. However, I have never agreed with the closure of Rivers Air Base. This is one of the last bases in Canada that should be closed.
In August of this year, the government announced the closure of two Manitoba bases, Gimli and Rivers. This left two air bases in Manitoba, Canadian Forces Base Winnipeg and Canadian Forces Base Portage. Why did these two remain open and why was Rivers closed? Canadian Forces Base Winnipeg is located adjacent to the Winnipeg International Airport and, needless to say, it causes much congestion of the air lanes in that area. This congestion is increased every day. If the government wants to save the taxpayers' money, why didn't they close Winnipeg instead of Rivers? Winnipeg Air Base is located in Greater Winnipeg and this property could be sold for millions of dollars. Rivers is located in the middle of the Prairies and the government will recover little of their investment on its closure.
Military men will tell you Rivers Air Base is in better condition than most bases in Canada. It has more days on which flying can be undertaken than any base in Manitoba. It is not situated close to the commercial air routes. It has all concrete runways. The permanent married quarters at Rivers are far superior to the ones, for example, at Portage. I can give you many reasons why Rivers should never have been closed.
For the last four years, delegation after delegation from Rivers and Western Manitoba have told the government these facts. But it is obvious the government was not prepared to listen to reason. The people of Rivers are annoyed, and they should be. Two years ago the former Minister of National Defence, told the people this base would not be closed. During discussions I had last spring
October 27, 1970

with the former minister of national defence he told me the British were prepared to lease Rivers Air Base for a training school. He said the British were driving a hard bargain but he thought a lease could be worked out. I suggested the Department of Regional Economic Development should become involved in the negotiations. Perhaps with some incentive from this department a deal could be worked out with the British. If the base were closed this government would have to spend thousands of dollars in trying to locate industry for Rivers. What better industry could there have been than 1,000 British troops training in Western Manitoba? This plan would permit the present maintenance staff to be kept on at the base. The government have never given any explanation of what happened to these negotiations with the British, Mr. Speaker; it is time they did.
After the crisis we have experienced in Quebec in the past month, the government will have to review its whole military policy. Not only has it been proven we are short of troops but now, apparently, we are short of air bases.
The government announced in August that Rivers Air Base would be closed by September, 1971. I understand the control tower at Rivers was closed on October 15. Then, only three days later, when troops from Camp Shilo had to be flown to Montreal, with great difficulty the tower at Rivers was re-activated. In the period of a day, I am told, nine Hercules and two Yukon planes came into Rivers to pick up troops and their equipment. Why did Rivers Air base have to be used? It was used because it is only 30 miles from Camp Shilo, one of the largest army bases in Western Canada. In addition, Rivers air base has concrete runways capable of handling these large transport planes that are necessary to move troops quickly in times of national emergency. Why was Portage air base not used, one of the bases the government has left open in Manitoba? Mr. Speaker, I say if the truth were known the Portage base, with its asphalt runways, cannot handle the large troop planes. Only last month I was informed a Hercules plane went through the runway at CFB Portage.
These events of the past ten days again make the people of Rivers and western Manitoba ask, why were the Winnipeg and Portage bases left open and Rivers closed? Was it at the expense of our national security? Was the government playing politics when they closed Rivers? I would hate to think so.
I strongly urge the government, Mr. Speaker, to tell the people of Rivers what the future of this airbase is. The announcement of its closure was made on August 25. At that time the Department of National Defence, the Department of Regional Economic Development and the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Richardson), who is from Manitoba, told the people of Rivers a suitable use would be found for the base and the government would assist in every way possible.
The people of Rivers have been getting the same runaround for the last four years. This community is being destroyed and many businesses have closed. Many homes are vacant and the economic prospects for this town are
Veterans Allowance Increases very gloomy. Why is it this way? Because the government will not announce what plans they have for Rivers.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I urge the government to tell the people of western Manitoba whether Rivers will be re-opened as a military base because of its strategic location. Is it to be turned over to the Department of Indian Affairs for vocational training? Is it to be turned into an industrial park so the Department of Regional Economic Expansion can locate industry there?

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-RECONSIDERATION OF CLOSING OF RIVERS AIR BASE
speechtext:
As I indicated to the hon. member when he asked the question, Mr. Speaker, the decision regarding the closure of Rivers base is final. It is not being reconsidered. The facts which the member referred to in his question, and again this evening, were fully taken into account when that decision was made. There will be no change in that decision.
The Canadian Forces Base Rivers, a flying training base, is being closed for financial reasons, that is to keep within the Department of National Defence budget. The airport was not re-activated, as the hon. member suggested in his question, because it had never been de-activated. While the manning of the control tower has been discontinued, the base will not close until September of 1971. For this particular incident, the control tower was manned by base personnel without any difficulty.
It was decided to use the airport because it was still active as a Canadian Forces base. When it is phased out, troops from Shilo will be able to move through Brandon airport. I should not lecture the hon. member on the geography of his own province, but Brandon is closer to Shilo than Rivers or CFB Portage. Indeed, in terms of proximity, Brandon is far more accessible than Rivers. I suggest to the hon. member that of the many reasons which from time to time have been advanced for keeping Rivers base open, the one he has referred to, namely that it can be used to move troops, is probably the least persuasive.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATED DAY, S.O. 58-VETERANS AFFAIRS-EARLY IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS AND WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE INCREASE
speechtext:
I am pleased Mr. Speaker, to be allowed to express my views on this most creditable and vital subject. I am sure the veterans in our society will take heart when they learn that the substance of the report of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs has come to the floor of this House for debate. I should also like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your consideration in extending the time available for debate on the subject in order that everyone who wishes to do so will be able to express his views today. I have sat in my place for most of the day and I have been heartened by the eloquence, the emotion and the sincerity which have been evident in all corners of the House. It does seem to me that this matter should have come to the floor of the House long ago. Certainly, any further delay would be inexcusable. If this debate proves to be just another false start on the road to the ultimate legislation, the government will find itself facing the full fury of both the members of this House and of the country at large.
A great deal has been said today about the valour of our warriors in past days. The fact is that no one can say sufficient about the sacrifices of our veterans to compensate them for the suffering and the hardships they endured. We must do far more than talk, though. I think we are all agreed that we must spice our words with action. Regardless of the war in which a veteran served, the present generation owes him the same debt as did those who lived in the same era. The sacrifices made by our soldiers, sailors and airmen have preserved our society, our sovereignty and our freedom for all the generations which followed them and the debt owed to those people is therefore passed along. The responsibility to bring veterans legislation up to date has fallen squarely on those of us who sit in Parliament today and it would be irresponsible of us to pass it along to anyone else. We must deal with it now in a manner in keeping with its character as an entitlement. I say "entitlement" because I want to speak out against the government's announced intention of holding back new veterans legislation until it has prepared an omnibus paper on the whole spectrum of social welfare legislation.
There are several reasons for my objection to this approach, not the least of which is the one I have just mentioned. Veterans compensation and pensions are totally unrelated to other types of benefits under welfare programs. The veterans of this country have earned certain entitlements which are uniquely theirs. Those entitlements are fundamental to our society and to our system of government. It is shabby and unconscionable, Mr. Speaker, to ask these people to stand in line for welfare to supplement inadequate pensions or compensation, because they paid for our freedom with their health and their limbs.
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel).]
Veterans benefits are not public welfare assistance and if all of the rest of my remarks become lost in the dark corners of the record, I want it to be remembered that I object most strenuously to any further delay in implementing legislation which will confer on our veterans adequate compensation, and confer it in a manner which will reflect the dignity with which they made their contributions. It is beneath our dignity as Canadians to do less than other nations are doing, and have done, for their veterans. It is beneath our dignity to strip the dignity from those who have given all they had to give and who now expect only what they have been led to expect. It is all too typical of this government to tell veterans that they will have to wait until they have been integrated into a vast bureaucratic jungle which will administer a multitude of unrelated situations, while at the same time playing down the significance of their contributions.
The hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott) pointed out a few days ago that the government seemed to be preoccupied with saying to hippies, yippies, draft dodgers and deserters: "Come to the promised land; come to Canada and work against our government and institutions". It is a sad commentary on our government, indeed on all of us, when we allow such a philosophy to take root in this land, a land made secure by the blood, pain and suffering of our own young men and women of past generations. It prompts one to ask whether there is anything left in Canada that is sacred. It is incomprehensible to anyone who has contributed and is now contributing to our society how government can take our hard won freedoms and institutions so cavalierly.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was only trying to impress upon the House the pressing need to give consideration to the needs of our veterans before those of other elements of society that seem to be coming to the forefront. I was going to mention U.S. draft dodgers, and I think this is pertinent to the discussion at hand. These deserters from the United States walk across an imaginary line between two countries and suddenly become something that they were not moments before they crossed the line. It is fundamental that a man cannot be expected to accept responsibility to a new society when he has demonstrated that he cannot accept responsibility to the society in which he grew up.
I contend a man owes a duty to the society that sheltered him while he was growing up. It is not enough to say that the debt has been discharged simply because an individual states that he disagrees with certain policies of his government. In a free society such as ours, there are established rules by which one must live. Without those rules, there would be chaos.
October 27, 1970

In the sort of society envisaged by most of our hippies and United States drop-outs, people who break the rules are put to death or at best sentenced to long terms of hard labour. I cannot accept lightly government policy that gives freely to such people the fruits of our labours and the benefits that we have derived from the sacrifices of our young people who accepted the responsibility of fighting to preserve our country both today and in times past.
There are elderly people in this country who are waiting to have their fixed and inadequate incomes brought into line with reality, with the present rather than the past cost of living index. There are those unable to work for a variety of reasons who must be looked after. There are also our veterans. It is cruel and inhuman for anyone to seek to sweep these human problems under the rug in order to get them out of sight and out of mind. I call on the government to deal with each of these problems separately, to stop trying to put them into a bag in the hope that when they are dumped out they will solve themselves.
Veterans legislation has always been kept apart from other legislation because it is different from anything else. It is no good for the government simply to say that all benefits are related, that no special conditions or considerations bear upon them. Veterans benefits have a special connotation. There are special considerations bearing upon them, and to ignore or deny these considerations is to do the veterans a disservice. The time to table legislation is now, not when the government has found a multitude of other problems to put together in an omnibus type of package. Our veterans are waiting for the answers and for some ray of hope. I call upon this government to use the majority it asked for and received at the last election to give our veterans the answers they want and require.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the veterans pension program was adopted some 50 years ago, Canada has witnessed drastic changes, economic as well as social. Being aware of this, the Department of Veterans Affairs had inquiries made in an attempt to adapt, to a greater degree, the services of the department to the veterans' requirements.
In spite of those efforts to humanize the services of the department, to adapt them even more to the needs of the pensioners, the fact remains that there are still scandalous injustices within that department, not where the civil servants or the officials are concerned, but because the pensioners cannot make ends meet with the help the department gives them.
Having said this, I would like to deal with another aspect which it seems to me has been neglected. The average age of the veterans of World War I being 74, and that of the veterans of World War II being 52, one can wonder what happens to their widows since, in most cases, because of illness or disability-because they
Veterans Allowance Increases fought proudly for Canada-they die prematurely. As a result, their widows and other dependants are very often destitute.
Mr. Speaker, the motion and the amendment aim at securing the adoption of many recommendations made by study committees.
One of those recommendations had to do with the wives and other dependents of pensioners, and I would like to be allowed to discuss it very briefly.
The cost of living is increasing steadily. All agree on that. The cost of medicine, housing and food has also increased. Thus, veterans and their dependents can no longer provide for their immediate needs.
Now since pensions are not adapted to the requirements of the people who receive them, some pensioners and their dependents manage very well to live on them, while others can barely subsist.
In my opinion, the pension given to veterans is insufficient. Indeed, the department is aware of that, for on June 30, 1965, it created a relief fund. It is called a relief fund because it is meant to be used to add a supplement to the monthly pension.
This fund is first intended to help the pensioners secure decent housing. In fact, inadequate housing and medical care for veterans' dependents, mainly those affected by chronic sickness, as well as the economic and social consequences of a death, are among the reasons why veterans are asking for the department's services.
Moreover, this fund is important since the financial assistance for special needs or maintenance of income is insufficient to allow pensioners to be self-sufficient or to fit into our society.
We now deal with the basic policy of the Department of Veterans Affairs which is to make it possible for the pensioner to meet his own needs and to adapt himself to this society which he defended so gallantly.
Finally, this fund has been created to meet the department's objectives, namely to achieve close co-operation between the various welfare organizations and to help veterans' widows and dependents.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
This prompts me to remind the hon. members that generally speaking pensioners' wives may not have had the chance to get an education or experience in handling domestic affairs, with the result that when the pensioner dies, the mother is left all by herself with no roof over her head and unable to earn her living because she never learned any trade and she lacks the experience and the know-how needed to handle her own affairs.
Mr. Speaker, the minister will say that hundreds of persons have been helped through this fund, and that it had quite willingly paid several million dollars. Nevertheless, I still maintain that this fund is being used unfairly and inadequately and that, actually, it merely serves as a front which is of no use to dependents or which serves as an excuse to convince the population that the department is taking good care of the dependents.

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases
But in fact, experience and the many cases we have witnessed prove that this reiief fund has not really assisted many people. I feel that is a pity because whereas pensions are intended to assist the veteran in readjusting to society, it is also necessary that, upon the veteran's death his dependents be assured of an income allowing them to continue living normally. They can certainly not be made to suffer the consequences of the war.
Mr. Speaker, I have in mind a case which came up this summer in the constituency of Lotbiniere. For several months, a woman from Victoriaville, the wife of a pensioner, appealed, through myself and through other persons, to the Department of Veterans Affairs for supplementary assistance because she was unable to meet her obligations. The department referred her case from one office to another. Finally, as her debts were piling up, she did not know where to turn. Eventually, her creditors called on her and through the bailiff, seized all her furniture. Being ignorant of the law and as she was desperately waiting for help from the special relief fund of the department, she was, at a moment's notice, turned into the street. The afternoon this happened, she came to my office to ask me whether I had heard from the department. When she left my office in Victoriaville to return home, she was at her wits' end. When she got home, she saw the decorations and war souvenirs of her husband as well as her own clothes in garbage bags. She tried to open the door but it was bolted.
For over six months we had been asking for help from the relief fund. All we had were false hopes-it must be said-and that person found herself in the street. She went to the chief of police in an attempt to get some protection but with no success.
We took the matter in hand and it looks as if we shall soon find a solution.
I submit this case to my honourable colleagues not with the intention of annoying them but rather to make them realize the importance of adopting a new policy within that department in order to humanize the services and adjust them to human needs.
The most urgent problem of pensioned veterans is the financial one. When the department realizes this, it will certainly be possible for them to face life more optimistically.
I urgently ask the minister to consider increasing pensions in order to bring them more in keeping with the cost of living, so that the pensioner, instead of being disadvantaged for having risked his life for his country, may live decently.
Also, the government should have more contacts with pensioners, in order to humanize its services and to treat pensioners as human beings and not numbers. There are 945,200 pensioners in Canada. It is impossible for the department to provide a human and personal service to the veterans with the present structures. Even if the department had enough money to help veterans, it should nevertheless reform its structures and humanize its services.
As there are 832,600 veterans from the Second World War and more than 112,600 from the First World War and only 29,800 pensions are paid to veterans or their dependents, the comments I have just made are of the utmost importance. If we want to help our veterans, we must leave no stone unturned to ensure the widow, the mother, the spouse or the dependents of the pensioner the same security as any civilian would have in a similar situation.
Mr. Speaker, if our government wants to be fair, it will deal in a more human fashion with those soldiers who went abroad to fight for their country. However, if it wants merely to grant pensions as it pleases, without regard to the individual needs of each family or to maintain only statutory services provided indiscriminately, I maintain that those services shall not achieve their purpose.
We should, in my opinion, humanize these services, so that scandals and glaring injustices, such as those suffered by the widow of a veteran in Victoriaville, do not happen again.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this debate rather belatedly. I had not intended to, but as the debate went on I could not help but be moved by many of the appeals and references that were made. It is rather interesting, because we are not a military people. This is not our tradition, and sometimes we are inclined to forget the value of the military and of those who have served. But in recent weeks I think many of us have become aware of the value and the outstanding service of the armed forces which serve in peacetime as well as in wartime.
There are times when we are really inordinately proud and grateful for the armed services, and I think the past few weeks have indicated their value to us in peacetime as well as in war. They have served with a quiet dignity, unobtrusively, in a vital role, efficient and well trained for the dreadful tasks which they have been called upon to fulfil, because of that role which is becoming traditional for them, that of peacekeepers.
I had to chuckle a bit at some of the rhetoric used in the debate. I do not mean this with disrespect, because I think back, Mr. Speaker, as you must think back 25 or 30 years to old friends who did not return, who are still there, who probably spoke of politicians who stood up in this House of Commons and chuckled and laughed at them, and probably would chuckle and laugh that you and I might be here now. They did not think of themselves as heroes. They died, sometimes heroically, sometimes otherwise. They were men, above all, who realized that war is not glorious. Some men are glorious in wartime and some are not.
I think of good Canadians, good Canadian names-I just started jotting down a few of them-who are still there: Leszinski, Sawyer, Worthington, Tessier, Rosenthal, Harris, Gugeon, Gagnon, Rayner, Stoll, Lefradi. This is a list of great Canadian names.
(Mr. Fortin.]

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even at this late hour I feel compelled to add some words to those that have been spoken today. The motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), is timely in that today has really been the first occasion upon which this House has had the opportunity of discussing veterans affairs after the report of the committee in June. This report was tabled in the House toward the latter part of that month and this subject was not discussed, and could not be discussed, on the general debate we had at the beginning of the session.
I think it is apposite that the House should be discussing today, on the first opposition allotted day, the recommendations of the committee. I had hoped to hear more discussion of the proposals in those recommendations instead of some of the very fine speeches which were made, which were really more in the nature of Remembrance Day speeches. By saying that I do not want to detract from them at all.
I want to underline one or two points that are strictly germane to the motion. First of all, in the report there is one unfortunate, shall we say, omission that has to do, not with the Hong Kong prisoners of war but with the ordinary prisoners of war. Of that group I think I am the only one who is a member of this House. Over the past several years, certainly when I was attending the committee at the time it was hearing representations with regard to the Woods committee report and on other occasions, I have made it a point to urge upon the ministry-and I was hoping during my brief tenure as head of that particular ministry several years ago to initiate the program about which I want to speak-the view that treatment services and/or the Pension Commission should organize a program of calling in all prisoners of war with respect to whom they might not have had a recent, complete medical report.
I had occasion this past summer to be involved with my regimental association. It is composed of members who served in World War I, of the 50th Battalion, and who served in World War II, of the King's Own Calgary Regiment. There I saw the changes in some of my older colleagues in that association and the changes in those of that regiment who are contemporaries of mine. One could see subtle signs, over the years, of some rather disturbing evidence of physical impairment. Some of those men
Veterans Allowance Increases were with me in prisoner of war camps and they are now suffering the accumulated results of the hardships of their experience.
It is not only about those in the army that I wish to speak. I want to talk about all those who were prisoners of war. It is fair to say that the air force prisoners far outnumbered the prisoners taken from the army-I am speaking of ground troops-yet strangely enough, a greater number of army troops have organized into associations which appeared before the committee through their duly appointed representatives. I want again to insist upon the urgency and the value of calling all these men, who are not recorded with the Pension Commission, who are not receiving pensions and who have not in recent years been in for a medical examination. This was done with regard to the Hong Kong prisoners of war. This is how that movement started.
I say without fear of equivocation that the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs were absolutely astounded by the results of the examination. Fortunately, they did not wait for those men to come in on their hands and knees suffering from the debility they now have. This is what we should do. We can get a salutary lesson or definition of what constitutes the long-term results of privation from men who were in this position for up to five years, and others for shorter periods but who had rather more severe experiences. That is my first point.
My second point is in connection with war veterans allowance. This has been a very sore point all along the line for many Canadians who are expatriates of this country, a great many from World War I and many more from World War II. I have personal knowledge of this matter and I have also heard the officials and representatives of the Canadian Veterans Association in the United Kingdom. These Canadian veterans would qualify for allowance except that they have not resided in Canada for the minimum period. They are denied the war veterans allowance. These people are suffering financially. They do not have the means to return to Canada for one year. Some are married and some have reached the ages of 65, 70 and over.
For some unknown reason there is a bureaucratic insistence that there will be a problem with Canadian veterans residing in the United States, flocking back to Canada. There would be no such problem. Nothing could be further from the truth. In my opinion it is an academic, administrative roadblock which has been set up to deny justice to these men living in the United Kingdom.
The government is prepared to pay war veterans allowance to members of allied forces who qualify and who are living in Canada, but denies this allowance to Canadian veterans living abroad. Some of these men married and are raising their families abroad. I do not understand why the government is continuing its blind persistence in denying these men that to which they are rightfully entitled.
My last point is the same as that raised by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). It is with regard to the Canadian parks and memorials in France

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases and Belgium. We hear disquieting rumours that for reasons of economy the administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs in London is being closed. Some of this administration is being transferred to the British ministry of pensions, and the parks and memorials will be transferred to the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.
I am sure Your Honour, as former chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, knows the value of memorials such as Vimy and how these memorials depend upon inspired Canadian maintenance and pride. I do not say this because the Commonwealth War Graves Commission cannot look after cemeteries; they are doing a tremendous job. But this is a real symbol for Canadians. If there is a symbol in Europe that portrays the valour and nationhood of Canadian forces during World War I, it is the Vimy memorial; yet we are prepared to transfer it. In any event, this is what we are informed is likely to be the case. I do not think it should be transferred to the Commonwealth War Graves Commission for maintenance and care. If it costs a little more, it is worth it. I commend this motion to hon. members and to the government for early action.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak for long at this late hour. What I have to say is the reiteration of what I have said in the House before, and what others have said. I support increases in war disability pensions and improvements for veterans at the earliest possible opportunity. In this regard I welcomed the tabling, on the opening day of the new session, of a list of measures projected for the session. Item 22 was entitled "Veterans pension legislation". Should this measure be introduced tomorrow, it would come none too soon for many of the veterans in this country.
A few weeks ago I visited the Beatty Street armoury in Vancouver. This armoury has been used during the summer months, very successfully most of the time, as a hostel for transient young people. However, when I called by on a spot-check, the administration of the hostel was clearly in trouble and unable to handle a situation wherein creatures known as yippies had descended like a baleful plague. This armoury, from which young men had been sent to at least three wars to defend democracy and, indeed, to defend the right to dissent in freedom, the right to join any or no political party, was occupied by a number of these people who had draped revolutionary flags and symbols over the monuments of the minders of Canada's military dead.

Your Honour's remarks really bring me to the point I was about to make. When I objected to what I considered to be acts of desecration, one strapping young man met my protest with the rejoinder, "It's a free country, isn't it?" I replied, "Yes, it is a free country; free because other young men, at other times laid their lives and their careers on the line and died to keep it free." But some lived; they came home with their bodies shattered and with their hopes for a productive, happy life, blasted. These are the people we are talking about in this debate. Many of them qualified for war disability pensions, pensions whose real purchasing power has declined steadily through the months and years. We have to do something for them now, soon, and I am confident that we will.
The report of the Veterans Affairs Committee was a good report. Its suggestion that there should be changes in the adjudication and appeal procedure was advanced with clarity and logic. Changes in the basic rate of pension were also proposed. I think we can all support proposals of this kind. Specific improvements were recommended. I repeat, the report was a good report. Now let us as legislators get on with the job-because deeds, not words, count at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief because I did not intend to take part in the debate.
I have carefully gone over the motion introduced by the official opposition.
As several of the previous speakers have pointed out, this is a very important motion, Mr. Speaker. I am not a veteran but having been in close contact with many of them over the years, I have become aware of their problems and the weaknesses of the present legislation or of its application.
From 1939 to 1945, the veterans of today were asked to defend, in Canada, or elsewhere, Christianity, civilization and democracy. Considering that only 27,800 pensioners, dependents or survivors now benefit from the veterans legislation, we understand why many of them are not satisfied with its application since they could never obtain anything.
Mr. Speaker, I want to recall that during the various inquiries, veterans have asked the government to amend the legislation in order to correct injustices. The first comment which I would like to make in this respect deals with appeals. On several occasions, I have noted that the present appeals system under the Veterans Act is absolutely antiquated and unfair, and this is due solely to an arbitrary bureaucracy.
On page 10 of the brief submitted to the Standing Committee of Veterans Affairs by the War Amputes of Canada, the following can be read:
The Canadian Association of the War Amputees of Canada accepts forthwith the conclusions of the Woods committee in this connection and asks the government to establish an independent Appeal Board ... Under the procedure now applicable to the Commission, no appeal can be made in such cases. One
October 27, 1970

commissioner alone studies the applications; he then obtains the signature of the two other commissioners. If the decision is negative, it is all over!
In another brief submitted by veterans themselves in 1969, there is reference to the establishment of an appeal board, and this time, the same recommendation appears at the beginning of the report submitted to the commitee. One can read in it the following:
... an appeal body above the Pension Commission.
Having studied the Speech from the Throne, we cannot wait for the establishment of this appeal board, nor for detailed changes in the administration of the veterans legislation. I keep on quoting:
Another basic principle in pension administration is that it is not only necessary to do justice but also to give the impression that justice has been done. The Woods Committee report shows clearly that under the present system where appeals are heard by the commissioners themselves, this impression is not given. An appeal board would fill this serious gap in the legislation. The Woods Committee has spoken highly of the comments of the Royal Commission on Governmental Administration (Glassco Commission) as to the necessity of protecting the citizens against arbitrary decisions rendered against them when they cannot appeal to administrative courts-
As it is the case for veterans, Mr. Speaker.
In his letter addressed to the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) on January 6, 1970, the chairman of the Veterans Committee of the Royal Canadian Legion was dealing with the same matter.
So, if the government has not seen fit to adopt all the recommendations contained in the briefs previously submitted by veterans associations, it should, I believe, at least accept the most urgent ones.
Before concluding, I wish to draw attention to the fact that the veterans-and God knows they are still willing to work when they are able to do so-should be able to profit from earnings gained through small jobs that they can still do in spite of the handicaps that the war has brought to them.
According to present legislation, when a veteran earns a supplementary income, his pension is discontinued so as to punish him for having had the courage to earn a few pennies.
At page 2 of the brief submitted by the war amputees of Canada in April 1969, section 2 reads as follows:
No interference and no obstacle should hamper the disabled veteran who wants to better his lot through a training course or any other apprenticeship in order to take peacetime employment, so that the money he earns through his remaining capacities should not in any way deprive him of his right to a pension. In other words, his pension is paid to him because of his disability in connection with the unskilled labour market. If he can earn his living with talents acquired through his remaining capacities, he should not suffer the smallest loss on account of it.
Mr. Speaker, it is not normal that veterans able to work because of their talents and good will should be penalized by a decrease in their pension as soon as they can earn money.
Veterans Allowance Increases If we want to keep the promises already made to the veterans when we asked for their services from 1939 up to 1945 in order to defend Canada, it seems to me that we should not deceive them today by forcing them to remain idle and by punishing them for the money they were courageous enough to earn.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to be the spokesman of the great number of veterans who reside in my riding. I remember that they used to invite me every year to the Remembrance Day ceremony in honour of their brothers who fell on the battlefield.
This year, this ceremony will take place on November 15.
[DOT] (11:10 p.m.)
I already know they are going to ask me to tell the government they want greater attention to the matter of the pension paid to them, which is clearly inadequate in a period of inflation.
I remember one veteran. In fact, I remember the day my brother, a soldier during the 1914-18 war, returned to Canada. The date was December 16, 1918. I was then five years old and had waited up until 1 a.m. to see him arrive. I had been making my mother tell me of what was going on, of the perils to which our soldiers were exposed. I was therefore anxious to witness the return of this man whom I barely knew since I was scarcely two years old when he had enlisted. I could hardly wait to see him with my own eyes and to hear with my own ears the tales he had to tell. My whole life was deeply influenced by those events. Since then I have always had the greatest respect for these brave young men who sacrificed the best years of their lives for the safeguard of our liberties.
We owe them a debt of deep gratitude and our most profound respect. We must pay them back not just with words but also with deeds. Effectively, we must give them the financial assistance needed to enable them to enjoy in their own right the privilege of liberty and security.
We may feel proud to say that our sons died on the field of honour. In Europe, our war cemeteries are well kept by the local populations. Last May I had the opportunity of visiting the one near Rouen, and I was quite impressed to see the great respect the people of this region have for Canadian soldiers, and the gratitude they feel for Canadian veterans who twice defended the freedom that they enjoy now.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the motion now under study and the related amendment should be supported by all members, because Canada can afford to grant greater benefits to veterans than those they enjoy now. This very evening, when I did not expect to participate in this debate, I had the visit of a veteran who told me of his problems.

I sincerely hope that Parliament will act more promptly, so that the older veterans may also, in the last years ol their lives, have the security and Ireedom lor which they have so valiantly lought. I am convinced that, in this way, we shall give their children definite prool that the country truly wants to recognize the sacrifices that their parents have made to preserve Ireedom.
That might also serve as an example lor our youth who could also be inspired by the confidence shown by the adults in their country, which they want to continue to build not lor the old who are going to die tomorrow
